explanation: The tongue gathers scent particles and delivers them to a sensing organ in the roof of the mouth. The fork lets a snake compare left and right to follow a trail.

claims.text: A snake flicks its tongue to collect scent chemicals from the air and the ground.
Snakes do not use their tongues to sense heat, cool down or feel vibrations; pit vipers sense heat with facial pits.
The tongue carries scent particles to the vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ in the roof of the mouth.
The forked tongue lets a snake compare scents on its left and right, which helps it follow scent trails.

evidence.restatement: Tongue-flicking samples odour molecules from the air and the ground.
The tongue is a chemical sampler. Snakes sense heat with pit organs (pit vipers, some boas and pythons) and vibrations through the jaw and inner ear, and they do not use the tongue to cool down.
The tongue tips deliver the particles to the paired vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ in the roof of the mouth.
The fork samples two points at once, so the snake can compare left and right and follow a scent trail.
